tools.title: Estimated Tax Safe Harbor Planner
tools.description: Use last year's total tax to estimate a safe-harbor baseline, then build a catch-up plan based on withholding and payments you've already made.
opening: If you have a W-2 plus 1099 income, or your income is lumpy, estimated taxes are rarely a math problem. They are a process problem.
This planner helps you build a conservative safe-harbor baseline from last year's return, then turn it into a clean catch-up plan you can actually execute (with an audit folder that makes sense).

sections.title: How The Planner Works
paragraphs: Step 1 is a baseline: last year's total tax times a safe-harbor percentage (usually 100%, sometimes 110% for higher income).
Step 2 is reality: you subtract withholding and payments already made.
Step 3 is execution: you spread what is left across the number of payments you still plan to make this year.
This does not replace a tax projection. It gives you a defensible floor so you can stop guessing and start tracking.

sections.title: When Safe Harbor Is The Right Move
paragraphs: Use a safe-harbor plan when your income is volatile, your deductions are uncertain, or you are mid-year changing your structure (new S corp, new rental, new business).
The safe-harbor mindset is simple: keep penalties off the table, then do the higher-leverage work (income shaping, documentation, and advisor packet quality).

sections.title: Common Mistakes That Blow Up Estimated Tax
paragraphs: Counting planned deductions that are not executed yet.
Assuming year-end cleanup will fix underpayments when cash flow is already tight.
Treating estimated taxes like a one-time event instead of a system you run every month.

faq.q: Is safe harbor always 100% of last year's tax?
faq.a: Often, yes. Higher-income filers may be subject to a higher safe-harbor percentage. This tool lets you model both so you can pick the more conservative floor.

faq.q: Do I have to make four equal payments?
faq.a: Many people do. If you are behind, the practical move is a catch-up plan over your remaining payments. This tool focuses on execution simplicity.

faq.q: What if my withholding is changing mid-year?
faq.a: Re-run the tool whenever your paycheck changes, you add a side income stream, or you shift profits between entities. Treat it like a monthly check-in.

tools.title: Home Office Reimbursement Calculator
tools.description: Calculate a home office reimbursement amount under an accountable plan using a simple square-foot allocation and a clean documentation checklist.
opening: A home office reimbursement done the right way is not about squeezing every dollar. It is about building a repeatable process your CPA can defend.
This calculator estimates a conservative reimbursement amount using a square-foot allocation, then gives you a documentation checklist so the math actually survives real-world execution.

sections.title: What This Calculator Is Actually Doing
paragraphs: You enter your home's total square footage and your dedicated office square footage to compute a business-use percentage.
Then you add the home expenses you want to reimburse (utilities, internet, rent, insurance, repairs, HOA, and similar).
The calculator allocates each expense by the business-use percentage, then suggests a monthly reimbursement cadence so you can stop doing year-end reconstructions.

sections.title: Execution Notes (Where People Get Burned)
paragraphs: If the space is not exclusive and regular, the math does not matter. The qualification gate matters first.
If you cannot show a simple policy, a reimbursement request, and contemporaneous receipts, your accountant ends up cleaning up a mess at tax time.
Keep it boring: monthly reimbursement, one folder per year, and the same worksheet every month.

sections.title: What To Hand Your CPA
paragraphs: A one-page accountable plan policy (effective date, what is reimbursable, and how reimbursements are requested).
Your square-foot calculation (floor plan or measurement notes, plus photos).
Expense proof (bills, receipts, statements) and a monthly reimbursement log.

faq.q: Is this the same as the home office deduction?
faq.a: No. This is a reimbursement workflow under an accountable plan. The point is a clean, repeatable process and documentation, not a one-off deduction.

faq.q: Do I need an S corp for this to matter?
faq.a: It often shows up in S corp conversations because reimbursements and documentation matter a lot there. The process quality is the real win.

faq.q: Should I reimburse yearly or monthly?
faq.a: Monthly is usually cleaner because it avoids reconstructing a story after the year ends. This tool shows both so you can pick a cadence you will actually follow.

tools.title: Augusta Rule Rent Calculator + Log
tools.description: Build a clean meeting log, estimate a defensible rent amount, and generate a simple CSV you can put in your audit folder.
opening: Most Augusta Rule problems are not math problems. They are documentation problems.
This tool is built for execution: estimate rent, stay inside the 14-day guardrail, and leave with a meeting log you can hand to your advisor without a long explanation.

sections.title: How To Use This Tool
paragraphs: Add your meeting dates, purpose, and attendees. The tool counts days and builds a simple log.
Enter a daily rate that is defensible for your area (based on comparable rentals or venue costs).
The calculator estimates total rent and flags when you are over 14 days so you do not accidentally convert a clean strategy into a mess.

sections.title: What Makes A Daily Rate Defensible
paragraphs: The rate is not whatever you want. It needs evidence.
Think like an auditor: could you show comps, invoices, or venue pricing that supports the number you used?
If you cannot defend it on paper, lower it and keep the process clean.

sections.title: What Goes In The Audit Folder
paragraphs: Meeting log (dates, attendees, agenda, minutes).
Comparable rate evidence (screenshots, quotes, or listings).
Payment record and entity approval notes (board minutes or consent).

faq.q: What happens if I use more than 14 days?
faq.a: The strategy changes materially once you exceed the guardrail. This tool flags it early so you can adjust before you create downstream problems.

faq.q: Do I need a formal meeting agenda and minutes?
faq.a: If you want the strategy to hold up in the real world, yes. The log, agenda, and minutes are the difference between a clean file and a sloppy story.
Yes. The tool generates a simple CSV so you can store it with your receipts and supporting evidence.
